Section 4.1 of Lock⁵ introduces the **hypothesis test**, the second big
inference tool of the book. A test weighs evidence for a *claim* about a
population — the **alternative hypothesis** ($H_a$) — against a default
**null hypothesis** ($H_0$) of *nothing going on* (no difference, no effect,
no association). Hypotheses are always statements about population
**parameters** (a mean $\mu$, a proportion $p$, a correlation $\rho$, or a
difference of two of these), never about sample statistics, and the null
hypothesis carries the equality. The logic is the same random-chance
reasoning as the bootstrap, run in reverse: we **simulate what sample
statistics would look like if $H_0$ were true** — for a randomized
experiment by re-assigning (permuting) the treatment labels at random, for
other tests by simulating from the null value — to build a
**randomization distribution** centered at the null value. If the observed
sample statistic falls in the unlikely tail of that null distribution, the
data provide evidence *against* $H_0$ and *for* $H_a$; Section 4.2 turns
that tail area into a formal **p-value**. The alternative may be
**one-sided** ($>$ or $<$, when the claim has a direction) or
**two-sided** ($\neq$, when it does not). The exercises below are from
*Statistics: Unlocking the Power of Data* (Lock⁵, 3rd ed., pp. 289–295):
Skill Builders 4.1–4.15 practice reading strength of evidence, stating
hypotheses, and checking their validity; 4.16–4.32 apply the ideas to real
studies; 4.33–4.39 ask whether an analysis even involves a statistical
test; 4.40–4.41 compare two ways of influencing voters. Where the printed
counts make it possible we run an actual randomization simulation
(10,000 permutations, seed 2026), and the ICU exercises use the
`ICUAdmissions` data from Data 2.3.

```{python}
#| include: false
import os
from pathlib import Path
_root = Path.cwd()
while not (_root / "_quarto.yml").exists():
    _root = _root.parent
os.chdir(_root)
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt, seaborn as sns
sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid")

def randomize(groups, stat_fn, reps=10000, seed=2026):
    """Randomization distribution: pool all values, permute them into groups
    of the original sizes (consistent with the null hypothesis of no
    difference between groups), apply `stat_fn` to the list of permuted
    groups, repeat `reps` times."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    pooled = np.concatenate(groups)
    sizes = [len(g) for g in groups]
    out = np.empty(reps)
    for i in range(reps):
        perm = rng.permutation(pooled)
        res, pos = [], 0
        for s in sizes:
            res.append(perm[pos:pos + s])
            pos += s
        out[i] = stat_fn(res)
    return out

def rand_plot(boots, observed, xlabel, bins=30, figsize=(6, 3)):
    """Histogram of a randomization distribution with the observed statistic
    marked by a vertical line."""
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=figsize)
    sns.histplot(x=boots, bins=bins, ax=ax, color="#4c72b0")
    ax.axvline(observed, color="#c44e52", lw=2)
    ax.set_xlabel(xlabel)
    ax.set_ylabel("Randomization statistics")
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

def rand_row(label, stat, boots, alternative="two-sided", digits=3):
    """One-row summary: observed statistic and randomization p-value."""
    if alternative == "two-sided":
        p = float((np.abs(boots) >= abs(stat)).mean())
    else:  # greater
        p = float((boots >= stat).mean())
    pdisp = "< 0.001" if p < 0.001 else round(p, 3)
    return pd.Series({label: round(float(stat), digits),
                      f"p-value ({alternative})": pdisp})

def yes_no(n_yes, n_no):
    """Binary array: 1 = yes/success, 0 = no."""
    return np.repeat([1.0, 0.0], [n_yes, n_no])
```

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Exercise 4.1

*(Skill Builder 1: testing whether the mean mathematics placement score is
greater than 25; dotplots of the four samples in Figure 4.4.)* Evidence
for "mean $> 25$" comes from samples centered *above* 25 — the further
above 25 (and the less the values straddle 25), the stronger the evidence.

- **(a) Sample A provides the most evidence.** Its scores run from about 24
  to 36 with a center near 30 — every part of the distribution sits above
  25, so a mean above 25 is hardly surprising even if scores vary.
- **(b) Sample C provides no evidence.** Its scores run from about 17 to 28
  with a center near 22 — *below* 25, the opposite direction from the claim.
  Samples B (center ≈ 26–27) and D (center ≈ 26–27) do point the right way
  and offer some evidence, but their values overlap 25, so the evidence is
  weaker than for Sample A.

## Exercise 4.2

*(Skill Builder 1: testing whether the mean service time at Restaurant #1
is less than at Restaurant #2; same-size samples, boxplots in Figure 4.5
with sample means shown as circles.)* Read off the circles: Sample A —
$\bar x_1 \approx 6$ vs $\bar x_2 \approx 9.5$; Sample B — $\approx 4.5$ vs
$\approx 12$; Sample C — $\approx 9$ vs $\approx 6$; Sample D —
$\approx 7.5$ vs $\approx 5.5$.

- **(a) Sample B provides the most evidence.** Its Restaurant #1 mean
  (≈ 4.5) is far below its Restaurant #2 mean (≈ 12) and the two boxplots
  barely overlap — a difference that big is hard to blame on chance.
- **(b) Samples C and D provide no evidence.** In both, the Restaurant #1
  mean is *higher* than the Restaurant #2 mean — the wrong direction for
  the claim. Sample A points the right way ($6 < 9.5$) but the heavy
  overlap means the evidence is only mild.

*(Skill Builder 1: testing whether the correlation between exam grades and
hours playing video games is negative; scatterplots in Figure 4.6.)*

- **(a) Sample A provides the most evidence.** Its points fall in a strong,

  negative but scattered, so it offers some evidence, just not strong.

## Exercise 4.4

*(Skill Builder 1: testing whether the proportion of US citizens who can
name the capital of Canada is greater than 0.75, based on samples of 40.)*
The sample results are A: 31/40 = 0.775, B: 34/40 = 0.85, C: 27/40 = 0.675,
D: 38/40 = 0.95.

- **(a) Sample D provides the most evidence** — 0.95 is far above 0.75.
- **(b) Sample C provides no evidence** — 0.675 is *below* 0.75, the wrong
  direction entirely.
- The simulation below shows why B is only moderate evidence: if truly
  $p = 0.75$, getting 34 of 40 correct happens about 9% of the time by
  chance, while 38 of 40 (Sample D) is very rare and 31 of 40 (Sample A)
  is common.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Null distribution of the sample proportion when p = 0.75 and n = 40, with the four sample results marked
rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
null_p = rng.binomial(40, 0.75, 10000) / 40
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3))
sns.histplot(x=null_p, bins=30, ax=ax, color="#4c72b0")
for x, name in [(27/40, "C"), (31/40, "A"), (34/40, "B"), (38/40, "D")]:
    ax.axvline(x, color="#c44e52", ls="--", lw=1)
ax.set_xlabel("Null sample proportions if p = 0.75 (n = 40), samples A-D marked")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
samples = pd.DataFrame({"Sample": ["A", "B", "C", "D"],
                        "Successes of 40": [31, 34, 27, 38],
                        "Sample proportion": [31/40, 34/40, 27/40, 38/40]})
samples["P-value if p = 0.75"] = [round(float((null_p >= ph).mean()), 3)
                                  for ph in samples["Sample proportion"]]
samples.round(3).to_string(index=False)
```

## Exercise 4.5

*(Skill Builder 2: state the hypotheses.)* Let $\mu_A$ and $\mu_B$ be the
mean of group A and of group B:

$$H_0: \mu_A = \mu_B \quad \text{vs} \quad H_a: \mu_A \neq \mu_B$$

The claim ("not the same") is nondirectional, so the alternative is
two-sided and the equality goes in the null.

## Exercise 4.14

*(Skill Builder 4: are these valid hypotheses?)*

- **(a) $H_0: \mu = 15$ vs $H_a: \mu \neq 15$ — Valid.** Hypotheses about a
  parameter, equality in the null, complementary and exhaustive.
- **(b) $H_0: p \neq 0.5$ vs $H_a: p = 0.5$ — Not valid.** The equality
  must appear in the *null* hypothesis; here the null contains no equality
  (and the "nothing different" statement sits in the alternative).
- **(c) $H_0: p_1 < p_2$ vs $H_a: p_1 > p_2$ — Not valid.** Neither
  hypothesis contains an equality, so together they leave out the case
  $p_1 = p_2$; the null hypothesis must include it.
- **(d) $H_0: \bar x_1 = \bar x_2$ vs $H_a: \bar x_1 \neq \bar x_2$ — Not
  valid.** Hypotheses are statements about population *parameters*, not
  about the sample means $\bar x_1$ and $\bar x_2$ (which are known once
  the sample is taken — no test needed).

## Exercise 4.15

*(Skill Builder 4)*

- **(a) $H_0: \rho = 0$ vs $H_a: \rho < 0$ — Valid.**
- **(b) $H_0: \hat p = 0.3$ vs $H_a: \hat p \neq 0.3$ — Not valid.** The
  hypotheses are written about the sample statistic $\hat p$ rather than
  the population parameter $p$.
- **(c) $H_0: \mu_1 \neq \mu_2$ vs $H_a: \mu_1 = \mu_2$ — Not valid.** The
  null hypothesis must contain the equality ("no difference"); here it is
  in the alternative instead.
- **(d) $H_0: p = 25$ vs $H_a: p \neq 25$ — Not valid.** A proportion must
  lie between 0 and 1, so $p = 25$ is impossible (presumably 0.25 was
  intended).

## Exercise 4.16

**How Compassionate Is Your Dog?** Dogs could push open a magnetic door to
reach their owner; owners were randomly assigned to call *help* in a
distressed tone (with crying sounds) or in a neutral tone (with humming).

- **(a)** Parameters: $p_D$, the proportion of all dogs in the *distress*
  condition that would open the door, and $p_C$, the proportion in the
  *control* condition:
  $$H_0: p_D = p_C \quad \text{vs} \quad H_a: p_D > p_C$$
- **(b)** Not strong enough evidence means the sample results are not
  surprising if the null is true: a difference in door-opening rates as
  large as (or larger than) the one observed could plausibly happen just by
  random chance, even if distress has no real effect. The data do not
  convince us that dogs open the door more often for a distressed owner.
- **(c)** Parameters: $\mu_D$, the mean time to open the door for all dogs
  in the distress condition, and $\mu_C$, the mean for the control dogs:
  $$H_0: \mu_D = \mu_C \quad \text{vs} \quad H_a: \mu_D < \mu_C$$
- **(d)** Strong evidence means a difference in mean opening times this
  extreme is unlikely to occur by random chance alone when $H_0$ is true —
  dogs really do react faster (open the door sooner) when their owner is
  distressed.

## Exercise 4.17

**Active Learning vs Passive Learning: Comparing Outcomes** Students in a
physics course were randomly assigned to an active-learning or a
passive-learning class period.

- **(a)** Parameters: $\mu_A$, the mean test score for all students taught
  with active learning, and $\mu_P$, the mean for passive learning:
  $$H_0: \mu_A = \mu_P \quad \text{vs} \quad H_a: \mu_A > \mu_P$$
- **(b)** Evidence supporting $H_a$ means active learners really do score
  higher on average — active learning leads to better actual learning of
  the material (not plausibly explained by random assignment chance).
- **(c)** For feelings of learning:
  $$H_0: \mu_A = \mu_P \quad \text{vs} \quad H_a: \mu_A < \mu_P$$
  where $\mu_A$ and $\mu_P$ are now the mean *feelings-of-learning*
  ratings for active and passive learners.
- **(d)** Evidence supporting this $H_a$ means students in the active
  classroom *feel* they learned less, on average, than students in the
  passive lecture.
- **(e)** **Active** learning appears best for actual learning, but the
  **passive** lecture makes students (incorrectly) think they learned more.

## Exercise 4.18

**Pesticides and ADHD** Urinary dialkyl phosphate (DAP, a pesticide marker)
was measured for 1139 US children, whose ADHD diagnostic status (Yes/No)
was also recorded — an observational study.

- **(a)** Parameters: $p_H$, the proportion of all children with *high*
  pesticide levels who would be diagnosed with ADHD, and $p_L$, the
  proportion with *low* levels:
  $$H_0: p_H = p_L \quad \text{vs} \quad H_a: p_H > p_L$$
- **(b) No.** The sample difference could be due to random chance — that is
  exactly the question a hypothesis test addresses: how likely is a
  difference this large in a sample of this size if the population
  proportions were really equal? Only if such a difference is unlikely
  under $H_0$ may we generalize the difference to the population.
- **(c)** Evidence supporting $H_a$ means chance is a poor explanation: in
  the population, children with high pesticide levels really are more
  likely to be diagnosed with ADHD. (The study is observational, so this
  establishes an association, not that pesticides *cause* ADHD.)

## Exercise 4.19

**Beer and Mosquitoes** In a randomized experiment in Burkina Faso, 25
volunteers drank a liter of beer and 18 drank a liter of water; mosquito
traps counted attractiveness to mosquitoes before and after consumption.

- **(a)** Parameters: $\mu_B$, the mean number of mosquitoes caught after
  consumption for all people who drink beer, and $\mu_W$, the mean for all
  who drink water:
  $$H_0: \mu_B = \mu_W \quad \text{vs} \quad H_a: \mu_B > \mu_W$$
- **(b)** Before consumption the beer group averaged
  $434/25 = 17.36$ mosquitoes and the water group $337/18 \approx 18.72$ —
  the beer group was actually slightly *lower*. The two means are
  different, but since the drinks had not yet been consumed, the
  difference must be the result of random chance in how volunteers were
  assigned — a good reminder that random assignment never balances groups
  perfectly.
- **(c)** After consumption the beer group averaged
  $590/25 = 23.60$ and the water group $345/18 \approx 19.17$ — the beer
  group is now higher by about 4.4 mosquitoes. This difference is the one
  the test targets; given the size of the study and that nothing changed
  for the water group, it is not the kind of difference we expect from
  random assignment alone.
- **(d)** If the part (c) difference is convincing, we conclude that beer
  drinkers attract more mosquitoes on average — the beer group's
  attractiveness went up after drinking, relative to the water group.
- **(e) Yes.** Volunteers were *randomly assigned* to beer or water, so the
  groups are alike in every other way; the only systematic explanation for
  the after-consumption difference is the drink itself. This randomized
  experiment supports the causal conclusion that beer consumption
  increases mosquito attraction.

## Exercise 4.20

**Guilty Verdicts in Court Cases** A reporter claimed 95% of court cases
that go to trial end in a guilty verdict; we sample 2000 such cases.

- **(a)** Parameter: $p$, the proportion of *all* court cases that go to
  trial and result in a guilty verdict. Statistic: $\hat p$, the proportion
  found guilty in the sample of 2000 cases.
- **(b)** The claim to be checked is $p = 0.95$, with no direction:
  $$H_0: p = 0.95 \quad \text{vs} \quad H_a: p \neq 0.95$$
- **(c)** Assessing evidence means asking: *if* truly 95% of all cases end
  in a guilty verdict, how likely is a sample proportion as far from 0.95
  as the one we observed, just by random chance of which 2000 cases land
  in our sample? If such a $\hat p$ is reasonably likely, the claim stands;
  if it is very unlikely, we have evidence that the true proportion is not
  0.95.

## Exercise 4.22

**Taste Test** 100 people taste two diet colas; we test whether *more*
people prefer Brand A.

- **(a)** Parameter: $p$, the proportion of all people (like these tasters)
  who prefer Brand A:
  $$H_0: p = 0.5 \quad \text{vs} \quad H_a: p > 0.5$$
  (No preference means a 50/50 split.)
- **(b) Strong evidence:** e.g., 90 choose Brand A and 10 choose Brand B —
  if preferences were really 50/50, a 90–10 split in 100 tastes would be
  almost impossible by chance.
- **(c) No evidence:** e.g., 48 choose Brand A and 52 choose Brand B — the
  result is on the wrong side of an even split.
- **(d) Inconclusive (some evidence, not strong):** e.g., 58 choose Brand A
  and 42 choose Brand B — more than half prefer A, but a 58–42 split could
  plausibly occur by random chance even with no real preference.

## Exercise 4.29

**Relationship between Income and Number of Children**

- **(a)** Parameter: $\rho$, the correlation between household income and
  number of children in the population of US households:
  $$H_0: \rho = 0 \quad \text{vs} \quad H_a: \rho \neq 0$$
- **(b) $r = 0.75$** shows more evidence of a relationship — the further a
  sample correlation is from 0, the harder it is to explain by random
  chance when $\rho = 0$.
- **(c) Neither — they show equal evidence.** $r = 0.50$ and $r = -0.50$
  are the same distance from 0; strength of evidence depends on the
  *magnitude* $|r|$, not the sign (the sign only gives the direction of
  the association).

**Red Wine and Weight Loss** In a hypothetical primate study, one group

- **(a)** Parameters: $\mu_R$, the mean resting metabolism rate for all

  necessarily conclude resveratrol works: the two boxplots overlap heavily
  and the mean difference (about 3) is tiny compared to the individual
  variability, so a gap this small could easily be random chance.
- **(c) Species B.** The sample sizes are the same and the resveratrol
  group again has the higher mean, but in Species B the gap is larger
  (≈ 57 vs ≈ 44) and the distributions barely overlap — with much less
  variability, random chance is a far less plausible explanation, so the
  evidence is stronger.

## Exercise 4.31

**The Lady Tasting Tea** Muriel Bristol-Roach claimed she could tell
whether milk or tea was poured into a cup first; Fisher designed an
experiment to test her.

- **(a)** In plain English: the null hypothesis is that Muriel has **no
  ability** to tell — she is just guessing, so she gets each cup right half
  the time by luck. The alternative is that she **can** tell the
  difference — she gets it right more often than chance would allow.
- **(b)** With $p$ the true proportion of times she guesses correctly:
  $$H_0: p = 0.5 \quad \text{vs} \quad H_a: p > 0.5$$

## Exercise 4.32

**Flaxseed and Omega-3** A company advertises that a tablespoon of milled
flaxseed contains, on average, at least 3800 mg of ALNA. Let $\mu$ be the
mean ALNA content per tablespoon (in the population of all tablespoons).

- **(a)** The company wants evidence that the average is *higher* than
  3800 mg (so the claim is safely supported):
  $$H_0: \mu = 3800 \quad \text{vs} \quad H_a: \mu > 3800$$
- **(b)** The consumer organization acts only if there is evidence the
  average is *less* than 3800 mg:
  $$H_0: \mu = 3800 \quad \text{vs} \quad H_a: \mu < 3800$$

Same data, opposite alternatives — which hypothesis is "the claim to
disprove" depends on who is running the test.

## Exercise 4.33

**Polling to determine average TV hours.** **No statistical test.** There
is no claim to assess — the poll simply estimates the average number of
hours a day people watch television with a confidence interval (or just
reports $\bar x$). Nothing is being challenged, so no null hypothesis.

## Exercise 4.34

**Polling about mobile homes.** **Yes, a statistical test.** Parameter:
$p$, the proportion of all people in the community living in a mobile
home; statistic: $\hat p$ from the 1000 people polled.

$$H_0: p = 0.10 \quad \text{vs} \quad H_a: p > 0.10$$

## Exercise 4.35

**Using the census about mobile homes.** **No statistical test.** The
census includes *every* resident, so the population percentage is known
exactly — if it is not greater than 10%, no evidence is needed; if it is,
no inference from a sample is required. (A hypothesis test only makes
sense when we must generalize from a sample to a population.)

## Exercise 4.36

**Right- vs left-hand reaction time.** **Yes, a statistical test.** Each
participant uses both hands, so the parameter is the mean *difference* in
reaction time: $\mu_d = \mu_R - \mu_L$, the mean (right − left) reaction
time for the population:

$$H_0: \mu_d = 0 \quad \text{vs} \quad H_a: \mu_d < 0$$

(The alternative is negative because "the right hand reacts faster" means
a *shorter* time for the right hand.)

## Exercise 4.37

**Braking reaction time in a simulator.** **No statistical test.** As in
Exercise 4.33, there is no claim to test — the study just estimates the
average reaction time.

## Exercise 4.38

**Coke/Pepsi taste test in New York City.** **Yes, a statistical test.**
Parameter: $p$, the proportion of all people (in NYC) who prefer Pepsi;
statistic: $\hat p$ from the random sample of tasters.

$$H_0: p = 0.5 \quad \text{vs} \quad H_a: p > 0.5$$

## Exercise 4.39

**Complete voting records of a county.** **No statistical test.** The
records cover *all* eligible voters in the county, so the proportion who
voted is known exactly — there is no sample and nothing to generalize.
Either more than 50% voted or they did not; no evidence is needed.

## Exercise 4.40

**Influencing Voters** 500 voters are randomly split: 250 get a recorded
phone call from the candidate, 250 get a mailed flyer; we test whether the
proportions who will vote for the candidate differ between the methods.

- **(a)** Parameters: $p_c$, the proportion of all voters who would support
  the candidate after a phone call, and $p_f$, the proportion after a
  flyer:
  $$H_0: p_c = p_f \quad \text{vs} \quad H_a: p_c \neq p_f$$
- **(b)** Sample A (Table 4.3):
  $\hat p_c = 152/250 = 0.608$ and $\hat p_f = 145/250 = 0.580$ — a
  difference of just 0.028.
- **(c)** Sample B (Table 4.4):
  $\hat p_c = 188/250 = 0.752$ and $\hat p_f = 120/250 = 0.480$ — a
  difference of 0.272.
- **(d) Sample B offers much stronger evidence.** If the two methods were
  equally effective, the success counts would be split between the 500
  voters essentially at random; the simulation below (pooling the
  successes and re-dealing the 250/250 group labels 10,000 times) shows
  that a difference of 0.028 (Sample A) is very ordinary under $H_0$ —
  $p \approx 0.59$ — while a difference of 0.272 (Sample B) never comes
  close to occurring by chance — $p < 0.001$.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Randomization distributions of the difference in proportions under the null of no difference, for Sample A and Sample B
phone_a = yes_no(152, 98)
flyer_a = yes_no(145, 105)
phone_b = yes_no(188, 62)
flyer_b = yes_no(120, 130)
boots_a = randomize([phone_a, flyer_a], lambda r: r[0].mean() - r[1].mean())
boots_b = randomize([phone_b, flyer_b], lambda r: r[0].mean() - r[1].mean())
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(7, 3))
for ax, b, obs, name in [
        (axes[0], boots_a, 152/250 - 145/250, "Sample A (diff = 0.028)"),
        (axes[1], boots_b, 188/250 - 120/250, "Sample B (diff = 0.272)")]:
    sns.histplot(x=b, bins=30, ax=ax, color="#4c72b0")
    ax.axvline(obs, color="#c44e52", lw=2)
    ax.set_title(name, fontsize=10)
    ax.set_xlabel("Randomization differences in proportions")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
pd.concat([rand_row("Sample A difference (phone - flyer)", 152/250 - 145/250, boots_a),
           rand_row("Sample B difference (phone - flyer)", 188/250 - 120/250, boots_b)],
          axis=1).to_string()
```

## Exercise 4.41

**Influencing Voters: Is a Phone Call More Effective?** Now 200 voters:
100 get the flyer, 100 get the phone call, and we specifically test
whether the phone call is *more* effective.

- **(a)** Parameters: $p_c$, the proportion of all voters who would support
  the candidate after a phone call, and $p_f$, the proportion after a
  flyer:
  $$H_0: p_c = p_f \quad \text{vs} \quad H_a: p_c > p_f$$
- **(b) Clear evidence** — a large difference in the right direction, e.g.:

  | Will vote for candidate | Yes | No |
  |---|---|---|
  | Phone call | 85 | 15 |
  | Flyer | 50 | 50 |

  A 0.35 advantage for the phone call would essentially never occur by
  random deal-out of the 200 voters if the methods were equally effective.
- **(c) No evidence at all** — the phone group does no better, e.g.:

  | Will vote for candidate | Yes | No |
  |---|---|---|
  | Phone call | 50 | 50 |
  | Flyer | 52 | 48 |

  The difference is 0.02 in the *wrong* direction, so it cannot support
  the claim.
- **(d) Not clear** — some evidence, but plausibly chance, e.g.:

  | Will vote for candidate | Yes | No |
  |---|---|---|
  | Phone call | 58 | 42 |
  | Flyer | 50 | 50 |

  The phone group does 0.08 better, but the simulation below shows a gap
  this size or larger happens in about a fifth of random deal-outs — some
  evidence, likely not strong enough to generalize.

```{python}
#| echo: false
examples = {"Clear evidence (85 vs 50)": (85, 50),
            "No evidence (50 vs 52)": (50, 52),
            "Unclear (58 vs 50)": (58, 50)}
rows = {}
for name, (nc, nf) in examples.items():
    b = randomize([yes_no(nc, 100 - nc), yes_no(nf, 100 - nf)],
                  lambda r: r[0].mean() - r[1].mean())
    obs = nc / 100 - nf / 100
    p = float((b >= obs).mean())
    rows[name] = [round(obs, 2), ("< 0.001" if p < 0.001 else round(p, 3))]
pd.DataFrame(rows, index=["Observed difference (phone - flyer)",
                          "p-value (one-sided)"]).to_string()
```
